Nabokov keeps this promise.  Throughout the rest of the commentary, Gradus’s journey from Zembla to Kinbote’s front yard – via Copenhagen, Paris, Geneva, Nice, Paris again, and finally New York – runs parallel to Shade’s composition of “Pale Fire.”  In his comment upon the very first line of the poem, which was begun “a few minutes after midnight July 1,” Kinbote admits that he is tempted “to synchronize a certain fateful fact, the departure from Zembla of the would-be regicide Gradus, with that date.”  In reality, we learn, the assassin left Zembla on July 5.ⁱˣ  Kinbote generally succumbs to the temptation of synchronization, and is rarely so forthright when it comes to his deployment of such wordplay.  A bit later in the book, for example, he describes Gradus approaching New Wye: “the force propelling him is the magic action of Shade’s poem itself, the very mechanism and sweep of verse, the powerful iambic motor.”ˣ Kinbote eventually admits that the synchronization of Gradus’s approach with the composition of Shade’s poem is just a literary device (and an overused one, at that), but the damage has already been done – our narrator has a problem delineating style from content.

Kinbote is a limited narrator that pretends to be omniscient.  His description of Gradus’s gradual approach is only one aspect of this trait.  We quickly learn that he has no problem filling the holes in his memory (of which there are many) with other, invented histories.  He obviously does not have extensive knowledge of Shade’s family history (he admits he has only known the poet for a few months, after all), but implies that he does through the invention of extended scenes set in and around Shade’s home.ˣⁱ  This implicative tendency can rightly be cited as a central reason for our distrust of Kinbote’s narration.

Pale Fire hinges upon Kinbote’s construction of a fictive history – the narrator cannot remember the past, and so fabricates one instead.  Nabokov further complicates our understanding of memory and reality in Pale Fire through his use of recurring language, persistent formal tics, and repeated details, all of which work together to cause memory-related glitches in the reader’s own head. For example, Kinbote brings up mirrors or instances of mirroring at least 10 times in Pale Fire.ˣⁱⁱ  We learn that the name “Zembla” translates as “land of resemblers”ˣⁱⁱⁱ and that a famous Zemblan mirror maker with the anagrammatic name “Sudarg of Bokay” once constructed a jewel-encrusted cheval glass for King Charles the Beloved’s grandfather.ˣⁱᵛ  Even the most unobservant reader cannot help but assume that all this talk of mirroring must mean something.  By the end of the novel, however, nothing is explained concretely.  We are left wondering about the significance of mirroring as a literary theme and hypothesizing about other possible examples of mirroring in the text.

It is easy, from this point, to begin to “explain” the book in terms of mirroring: Kinbote alone might be read as a sort of mirror image of Shade, King Charles, Gradus, or Hazel.  Looking elsewhere for mirrors, there are obvious parallels to be drawn between Kinbote and Nabokov himself.  Both were exiled from Communist countries, both taught at small universities (Nabokov at Cornell) in the New England area, and both, at the most basic level, are writers.  This comparison is openly encouraged by Kinbote when he writes, “I may turn up yet, on another campus, as an old, happy, healthy, heterosexual Russian, a writer in exile…”ˣᵛ  Finally, Kinbote might easily be read as a mirror image of us, the readers of Nabokov’s Pale Fire.  On a very literal level, he misreads Shade’s poem egomaniacally, inserting himself into the narrative whenever he gets the chance.  After digesting Pale Fire, it is hard not to think that we are doing the same thing.

The book actively promotes disorientation and paranoia in its readers.  Whenever it seems that a unifying narrative explanation is looming, Kinbote proceeds to complicate things even more.  On page 272, for example, he inadvertently describes the form of the book in which he is a character: “…our poet suggests here that human life is but a series of footnotes to a vast obscure unfinished masterpiece.”ˣᵛⁱ  It seems like this line should have serious consequences in the world of the book, and that it should tell us something important about Kinbote and his narrative voice.  Any conclusions we reach because of quotes like this, however, are ultimately inferred and not necessarily present in the text.

Although we have spent much time pointing out Kinbote’s many narrative failures, the fact remains that his is the only narrative voice in Pale Fire.  Even Shade’s poem has been filtered through his head.  Everything we say about him, then, must have originated with him at some point. No matter how hard we try to see through his narration to some hidden “real” world underneath, we will ultimately only come face to face with his own words.  On page 261, Kinbote quotes Franklin Lane and inadvertently describes what we want most in the book:

And if I had passed into that other land, whom would I have sought?...Aristotle! – Ah, there would be a man to talk with!  What satisfaction to see him take, like reins from between his fingers, the long ribbon of man’s life and trace it through the mystifying maze of all the wonderful adventure….The crooked made straight.  The Daedalian plan simplified by a look from above – smeared out as it were by the splotch of some master thumb that made the whole involuted, boggling thing one beautiful straight line.ˣᵛⁱⁱ

Kinbote is completely incapable of “explaining” the events in Pale Fire – he cannot make “the whole involuted, boggling thing one beautiful straight line.”  What he can do and does do, in fact, is show us his own path through the maze.  Kinbote’s own version of “Pale Fire” (and Pale Fire, for that matter) is probably not the one that we would choose (had we been offered the choice), but it is the one we are stuck with.  To be succinct: Kinbote’s narration, even though it comes from a seriously flawed memory, is the basis of all authority in Pale Fire.  By reinventing the past, Kinbote seriously and permanently influences the future.

Pale Fire effectively demonstrates the power of a single narrative voice to alter history forever, and so to gain great authority in the present.  This idea holds great implications for many disciplines outside of literature, especially in those fields that rely heavily on narrative. That said, literature in general and the novel in particular are exceptionally capable of pointing out this detail – more so, I believe, than any other discourse.  Nabokov describes the essential character of the written word when he writes:

We are absurdly accustomed to the miracle of a few written signs being able to contain immortal imagery, involutions of thought, new worlds with live people, speaking, weeping, laughing.  We take it for granted so simply that in a sense, by the very act of brutish routine acceptance, we undo the work of the ages, the history of the gradual elaboration of poetical description and construction, form the treeman to Browning, from the caveman to Keats.  What if we awake one day, all of us, and find ourselves utterly unable to read?  I wish you to gasp not only at what you read but at the miracle of its being readable.ˣᵛⁱⁱⁱ

The very existence of language and the consequent work that it does for us is proof of its ultimate authority.  In the same way that Kinbote controls and restrains any understanding we think we have of Pale Fire, language inherently mitigates our understanding of the so-called “real” world. Ultimately, then, we are only capable of choosing our own path through the maze.
